gaps.sentence: There weren't ___ chairs, so some guests had to stand.
gaps.explanation: 'Chairs' is countable and plural, so 'many' fits; 'much' and 'little' are for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: ___ the rooms in the hotel have a sea view; the rest face the car park.
gaps.explanation: Before 'the rooms' a partitive is needed: Some of; 'all/none' contradict the context.

gaps.sentence: The lecture was ___ attended than the organisers had hoped.
gaps.explanation: 'Well attended' compares with the adverb: less well attended.

gaps.sentence: This is ___ beautiful beach on the island.
gaps.explanation: 'The most beautiful' is the superlative form used for comparisons within a group.

gaps.sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

gaps.sentence: We see our grandparents ___ other weekend.
gaps.explanation: 'Every other weekend' means alternate weekends; 'each other' has a different, reciprocal meaning.

gaps.sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
gaps.hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
gaps.explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.
'Luggage' is an uncountable noun, so 'how much' is used.
